A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Block-Attention research, despite the revised title and expanded scope. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v4 has no appendix; v5's Appendix A is available and included.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original RAG accuracy experiments, ablations, training curves, and latency/FLOPs measurements in Tables 1-2 and Figure 4.

after.justification: Section 3 reports RAG, general-capability, and in-context-learning experiments. Appendix A additionally reports original latency outcomes from an internal game application.

M1.justification: v4 adapts models through block-mask fine-tuning. v5 explicitly trains every training sample under both block and full attention to preserve both operating modes, substantially changing the training procedure. It also specifies segmentation of general SFT examples by turns, messages, and delimiters. The underlying block mask, cache reuse, and RoPE operations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v5 adds Tulu3 SFT training data, seven reported general/ICL benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, DROP, MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval, and IFEval), and an internal game scenario in Appendix A. The four original RAG benchmarks remain. NarrativeQA is also named, but its actual evaluation is unclear because no corresponding results are reported.

E2.justification: The reported comparison set expands to include Superposition and an original Tulu3-SFT control alongside the RAG-fine-tuned full-attention baseline. PromptCache was already evaluated in v4 through results identified as identical to its weak baselines; v5 reports it separately from block-without-fine-tuning, with distinct outcomes. The no-fine-tuning and no-position comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Sections 3.1-3.4 replace Llama3-8B/Mistral-7B with Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT and replace GPT-4-generated RAG answers with Llama3.3-70B-Instruct answers. Added evaluations use zero-shot general tests, four-shot GSM8K/MATH, and three-shot BBH/DROP. Hardware is reported as eight H20s rather than eight A800s; this does not establish that the unchanged timing results were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 adds a full-attention fallback ablation testing whether the block-trained model retains compatibility with full attention. Figure 4 changes from comparing separately trained models to comparing two attention modes of the adapted model. Existing fine-tuning and positional ablations remain, while Appendix A adds a game-state reuse case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Benchmark averages and checkpoint curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The Llama3/Mistral accuracy table is replaced by Tulu3 results, and seven-task results are added. Figure 4's reported adaptation point changes from about 400 to 800 steps under different training conditions. Appendix A reports TTFT decreasing from 2,800 to 100 ms. These are new or replaced results, not same-setting improvements over v4. The original latency/FLOPs table is numerically unchanged, moving from Table 2 to Table 3.

T1.justification: The KV-state definitions and RoPE derivation in Equations 1-3 are unchanged. Appendix A's conditional-probability notation illustrates game tasks but adds no substantive mathematical reasoning, formal assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: v4's central validation concerns maintaining RAG accuracy while reducing prefilling cost. v5 broadens the claimed contribution to general and ICL capabilities, adds lossless switching between block and full attention as a central claim, and highlights game-AI applications in the abstract. The headline 32K latency/FLOPs reduction claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v5 interprets joint training as enabling both attention modes and removes v4's conjecture that passage independence might make block attention intrinsically more accurate. PromptCache's critique shifts from restrictive cache reuse to positional-encoding-related quality degradation. Discussion emphasizes real-time game agents instead of ReAct, and a new qualification explains the absence of subjective evaluations requiring OpenAI API access.

D1.justification: v5 announces public code, datasets, and model weights and supplies a project access link. It documents Tulu3 segmentation rules, the usable 23% fraction, and OpenCompass evaluation. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v4's explicit DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage-2 and Flash-Attention V2 specifications are omitted.

R1.justification: A new concurrent-work section credits TurboRAG's independent similar contribution and distinguishes the approach from DecoupledRAG, NSA, and MoBA. Parallel-context positioning expands through Superposition, SGLang, and CacheBlend. The earlier general discussion of linear attention, mixture-of-experts, speculative decoding, and RAGCache is removed; PCW's duplicate references are consolidated.

P1.justification: The title changes from Efficient RAG to Efficient Prefilling. The abstract, experimental narrative, baseline descriptions, and results discussion are substantially rewritten. Related work is reorganized into three subsections, and acknowledgements and a game appendix are added. Author, affiliation, conference-header, and attention terminology edits accompany this restructuring.

P2.justification: v5 adds the general/ICL Table 2 and game illustration Figure 5. Table 1 drops the three average columns and reorders datasets. Figure 4 is redrawn with revised axes, legends, and curves; Figures 2 and 4 use text-wrapped placement. The unchanged efficiency table is relocated and renumbered Table 3.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens practical validation by directly testing general-capability retention and switching back to full attention, concerns left untested in v4. The switching ablation, general/ICL evaluations, additional comparator, and new resource-access information improve evidential coverage and reproducibility. These gains are tempered by losing Mistral coverage, limited game-experiment documentation, and overstated accuracy claims: Section 3.5 claims RAG gaps of at most 1%, while Table 1 reports HQA scores of 72.3 versus 74.8. These weaknesses limit the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial added validation.
